A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# @webframp/redmine

Redmine issue tracker integration for swamp. Manage issues, projects, and
workflows through the Redmine REST API. Provides model methods for CRUD
operations on Redmine issues (themes, stories, tasks), project queries,
status/tracker/user lookups, and custom field access. Includes reports for flow
metrics (cycle time, lead time, throughput, WIP age) and sprint summaries, plus
a scaffold-story workflow for creating stories with child tasks.

## Prerequisites

- A running [Redmine](https://www.redmine.org/) instance with the REST API
  enabled
- A Redmine API key (found under My Account in Redmine)
- [swamp](https://github.com/systeminit/swamp) CLI installed

## Installation

```bash
swamp extension pull @webframp/redmine
```

## Usage

### Create a model instance

```bash
swamp model create @webframp/redmine tracker \
  --global-arg host=https://redmine.example.org \
  --global-arg apiKey=YOUR_API_KEY \
  --global-arg project=my-project
```

### List issues

```bash
swamp model method run tracker list_issues \
  --arg statusId=open \
  --arg sort=updated_on:desc
```

### Get a single issue with journals and children

```bash
swamp model method run tracker get_issue --arg issueId=1234
```

### Create an issue

```bash
swamp model method run tracker create_issue \
  --arg subject="Fix login timeout" \
  --arg trackerId=1 \
  --arg priorityId=2 \
  --arg description="Users report session timeouts after 5 minutes"
```

### Update an issue

```bash
`list_users`, `create_issue`, `list_versions`, `create_version`, and
`list_issue_categories` require a project identifier. If `project` is not set in
global args, you must pass it per-method or the method throws.

### `update_issue` re-fetches after mutation

The method performs a PUT then re-fetches the issue via GET to return the
updated state. If the re-fetch fails after a successful update, the mutation
succeeded but the method throws (no resource written).

### `upload_file` reads the local file path

The `filePath` argument must be an absolute path readable by the swamp process.
If the file cannot be read, the method throws with the path in the error
message.

### Reports and workflows referenced in README do not exist here

The README documents reports (`flow_metrics_report`, `sprint_summary_report`)
and a workflow (`scaffold-story`) that live in the separate
`@webframp/redmine-kanban` extension, not this one.

## License

Apache-2.0 -- see [LICENSE.md](LICENSE.md) for details.
## 2026.10.20.1

**Added:** `list_attachments` lists the attachments of an issue (ID, file name, size, content type, author, date) into a new `attachments` resource, named `attachments-<issueId>`. `download_attachments` downloads them in one run into a new `attachment` file spec, named `attachment-<issueId>-<attachmentId>`, with filters for attachment IDs and a content-type prefix, and a `maxBytes` limit (default 20 MiB). Until now the type had no way to read an attachment: `get_issue` does not request `include=attachments`, and `upload_file` was the only file method.

**Upgrade note:** No `globalArguments` changes; existing instances move to this version with an identity upgrade. Downloads send `X-Redmine-Username` when `username` is set, like every other method, and retry 429/502/503/504 like the JSON helpers.

-**Fixed:** `redmineApi`/`redmineApiPaginated` had no retry logic — any 429
-(or 502/503/504) failed the request outright. A caller sequentially fetching
-many issues (e.g. an enrichment step iterating over a large ticket list) can
-trip Redmine's rate limiter even at concurrency 1, and every prior release
-turned that into a hard failure. Both helpers now retry through a shared
-`fetchWithRetry`, honoring `Retry-After` when the server sends one and
-falling back to exponential backoff (up to 4 retries) otherwise.

+Redmine's rate limiter even at concurrency 1, and every prior release turned
+that into a hard failure. Both helpers now retry through a shared
+`fetchWithRetry`, honoring `Retry-After` when the server sends one and falling
+back to exponential backoff (up to 4 retries) otherwise.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/sme/.claude/skills/pre-push-review

# Pre-Push Review Loop

Run a local adversarial review on uncommitted or unpushed changes. Iterate
until the review passes, then stop and ask the human for push confirmation.

## When to Use

After making changes and before pushing to a remote branch. Especially
critical for:
- Fixes to prior adversarial review findings (regression risk is high)
- Concurrent-access code (locks, sequences, distributed state)
- Any change touching error handling or fallback paths
- New code (>200 LOC) — fresh code has too much surface area for a single pass

## The Loop

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                     │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌───────────┐    ┌──────────────┐ │
│  │  SHOW    │───►│   RUN     │───►│  EVALUATE    │ │
│  │  DIFF    │    │  GATES    │    │  VERDICT     │ │
│  └──────────┘    └───────────┘    └──────┬───────┘ │
│                        ▲                 │         │
│                        │           ┌─────┴─────┐   │
│                        │           │           │   │
│                        │         PASS        FAIL  │
│                        │           │           │   │
│                        │           ▼           ▼   │
│                        │     ┌──────────┐ ┌──────┐ │
│                        │     │  ASK TO  │ │ FIX  │ │
│                        │     │  PUSH    │ │      │ │
│                        │     └──────────┘ └──┬───┘ │
│                        │                     │     │
│                        └─────────────────────┘     │
│                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Phase 1: Show Diff

Collect the changes to review:

```bash
# Uncommitted changes against HEAD:
git diff HEAD

# Or unpushed commits against remote:
git diff origin/main...HEAD
```

Use whichever is appropriate. If there are uncommitted changes, review those.
If all changes are committed but unpushed, review the full branch diff.

## Phase 2: Run Quality Gates

Before sending to the reviewer, verify the code compiles and passes local
checks. This phase has two parts: standard gates and repo-specific gates.

### 2a. Standard Gates

Discover gates from the project's config files:

| Config file | Commands |
|-------------|----------|
| `deno.json` | `deno task check && deno task lint && deno task fmt:check && deno task test` |
| `package.json` | `npm run lint && npm run build && npm test` |
| `Cargo.toml` | `cargo check && cargo clippy && cargo test` |

If gates fail, fix them first. Do not send broken code to the reviewer.

### 2b. Repo-Specific CI Gates

Standard gates catch compile/lint/test failures. They do NOT catch structural
or convention failures that CI validates separately.

**Always check for repo-level guidance first.** Read steering files, skills,
CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, or contributing docs in the target repository. These
define what CI expects beyond standard compilation. Follow that guidance
exhaustively — run EVERY command listed, not a subset. Skipping a single
command from the checklist is the same as skipping Phase 2 entirely.

If no explicit guidance exists, fall back to these heuristics:

1. **Check CI workflow files** (`.github/workflows/`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`).
   Identify validation steps beyond standard gates and run them locally.

2. **Compare directory structure against a peer.** In repos with many
   packages of the same kind, your new addition must match the structure
   of existing ones (marker files, metadata files, test file conventions).

3. **Run repo-specific validation commands locally.** If CI runs a
   validation command, run it yourself first.

**The principle:** if CI will run it, you run it first. "It compiled and
the tests passed" is necessary but not sufficient.

### 2c. Swamp Extension Version and Manifest Gates

When changes touch swamp extensions (any directory with a `manifest.yaml`),
run these additional checks BEFORE the adversarial review. These fail
frequently and are easy to miss:

1. **Version alignment.** The `version` field in `manifest.yaml` MUST match
   the `version` field in the model's TypeScript source (`export const model =
   { version: "..." }`). If you bumped the model version, bump the manifest.
   Verify with `swamp extension version --manifest manifest.yaml --json`.

2. **Upgrade chain integrity.** If the model has an `upgrades` array, the last
   entry's `toVersion` MUST equal the model's `version` field. Every upgrade
   entry MUST have a unique `toVersion` in ascending order. A version bump
   without a corresponding upgrade entry means cached data from the previous
   version will not be migrated.

3. **Manifest format validation.** Run `swamp extension fmt manifest.yaml
   --check --json`. This catches YAML formatting issues that the push rejects.

4. **Quality gate.** Run `swamp extension quality manifest.yaml --json`.
   Verify `status: "passed"` and no degraded checks.

5. **Dry-run push.** Run `swamp extension push manifest.yaml --dry-run`.
   This exercises the full bundler, archive builder, and schema validation
   pipeline. If it fails here, it fails in CI.

**Common failure modes:**
- Bumping `model.version` but not `manifest.yaml` version
- Adding an upgrade handler but using the wrong `toVersion` string
- Forgetting to add `days` or `fetchedAt` to a new resource spec that
  requires it (schema validation fails on push)
- Leaving the old spec name in a `writeResource` call after renaming specs

## Phase 3: Adversarial Review via Subagent

The subagent MUST have the same capability as a CI adversarial reviewer.
A diff blob with prose context is insufficient — the reviewer must read
the actual source files to trace execution paths, verify cross-function
consistency, and find protocol-level issues.

### Subagent Setup

Use a general-purpose subagent (fresh context, read access to the repo). Provide:

1. **File paths to read** — tell the subagent which source files to read
   in full. The diff identifies *what* changed; the source files reveal
   *what interacts with* what changed. The subagent must read the complete
   implementation files, not just the diff.

2. **The diff** — for awareness of what's new vs existing code.

3. **Protocol and boundary context** — describe the external system's
   interface contract. For APIs: how input is parsed (line-delimited?
   shell-tokenized? JSON?). For CLI wrappers: how arguments are
   concatenated. For network protocols: framing, escaping, delimiters.
   The reviewer cannot find injection bugs without understanding the
   protocol boundary.

4. **Sibling consistency requirement** — if the code has multiple
   functions that do similar things (e.g., multiple command builders,
   multiple SSH invocations), explicitly instruct the reviewer to verify
   that ALL siblings apply the same validation/escaping/timeout patterns.
   Inconsistency between siblings is the #1 class of bug that single-pass
   reviews miss.

### Review Prompt Requirements

The subagent's review instructions MUST include these specific probes
(not just "assume broken"):

1. **Trace every interpolation site.** For each user-supplied value that
   ends up in a command string, network request, or file path: what
   characters can break the framing? Spaces, newlines, quotes, semicolons,
   pipes, backticks, dollar signs, null bytes — each has meaning in
   different contexts.

2. **Verify sibling consistency.** If function A validates input X, do
   ALL functions that accept the same class of input apply the same
   validation? List every sibling and confirm.

3. **Check timeout/resource bounds on every external call.** Every
   subprocess spawn, every network request, every fan-out: is there a
   hard deadline? What happens if it hangs? What happens if output is
   unbounded?

4. **Test with concrete breaking inputs.** For each finding, provide the
   exact input string that breaks it. "This could be a problem" is not a
   finding — "input X produces output Y which the server interprets as Z"
   is a finding.

5. **Verify the bootstrap/lifecycle path.** Can the code be invoked in
   the order the documentation describes? Are there circular dependencies
   between configuration and the methods that produce that configuration?

6. **Check truthiness vs nullability.** In JavaScript/TypeScript,
   `if (x)` skips `0`, `""`, `NaN`, `null`, `undefined`. For numeric
   parameters, `0` is often a valid value. For optional strings, `""`
   may be meaningful.

7. **Check for deferred work.** Does the change exclude, skip, stub, or
   TODO something the author identified as broken? Does the PR description
   or a code comment contain "follow-up", "until X handles it", "known
   limitation", or "out of scope" for a defect in the code being touched or
   sharing its root cause? A fix that avoids the defect (exclusion list,
   feature flag off, narrowed scope) instead of fixing it is a HIGH finding
   unless the user explicitly approved the deferral. Verify each claim the
   description makes about why the work was not done against the actual
   spec/code; a deferral rationale that is factually wrong is CRITICAL.

### Verdict Format

Require the subagent to produce:

```
### [CRITICAL|HIGH|MEDIUM|LOW] <title>
**File:** <path>
**Line(s):** <range>
**Issue:** What is wrong
**Breaking input:** The exact value that triggers the bug
**Impact:** What breaks
**Fix:** How to fix it

## VERDICT: PASS or FAIL
```

FAIL if any CRITICAL or HIGH findings exist. PASS otherwise.

## Phase 4: Evaluate Verdict

| Verdict | Action |
|---------|--------|
| PASS (no HIGH+) | Proceed to Phase 5 |
| FAIL (any HIGH+) | Fix findings, return to Phase 2 |

### On FAIL

- Fix ALL findings (HIGH, MEDIUM, and LOW). Do not defer.
- After fixing, re-run quality gates (Phase 2)
- Re-run the adversarial subagent (Phase 3) on the CURRENT source files
- The re-review MUST re-read the source files — do NOT just re-review
  the new diff. Fixes often introduce new inconsistencies.
- Do NOT push between iterations

### Minimum Iterations

- For new code (>200 LOC of implementation): run at minimum 2 review
  iterations even if the first passes. Fresh code has too much surface
  area for a single pass to catch everything.
- For fixes to existing code (<50 LOC): one passing iteration is
  sufficient.

### Iteration Cap

Maximum 5 review iterations. If still failing after 5:
- Summarize what was fixed
- List remaining findings
- Ask the human for guidance — do not push in a failing state

## Phase 5: Ask to Push

When the review passes:

1. Show a brief summary of what changed
2. State: "Local adversarial review passed. Ready to push?"
3. **Wait for explicit human confirmation**
4. Only push after the human says yes

## Rules

- NEVER push without human confirmation, even on PASS
- NEVER skip Phase 2 (quality gates) — broken code wastes review cycles
- NEVER send only a diff to the reviewer — the subagent must read the
  full source files. A diff is supplementary context, not the primary input.
- NEVER defer a finding. Fix ALL findings before the next iteration.
  Deferral is not your decision — only the human can choose to ship with
  a known issue. If you think something should be deferred, ask
  explicitly. Otherwise, fix it.
- If the same finding appears twice across iterations, try a fundamentally
  different approach rather than tweaking the same fix
- After fixing findings, the re-review must check that the fix didn't
  introduce inconsistency with sibling code. Fixing function A without
  applying the same fix to sibling functions B and C is the most common
  regression pattern.
- The subagent review has confirmation bias limitations (it reads with
  fresher eyes than you, but still runs on the same model). Expect CI to
  occasionally catch things the local loop misses — but "occasionally"
  means one finding, not six rounds of fixes. If CI finds more than one
  HIGH after your pre-push loop, the loop was run incorrectly.
Phase 2c: swamp manifest gates.

## 2026.10.20.1

**Added:** `list_attachments` lists the attachments of an issue (ID, file name,
size, content type, author, date) into a new `attachments` resource, named
`attachments-<issueId>`. `download_attachments` downloads them in one run into a
new `attachment` file spec, named `attachment-<issueId>-<attachmentId>`. It
filters by attachment IDs or a content-type prefix (case-insensitive) and skips
files over `maxBytes` (default 20 MiB). Until now the type had no way to read an
attachment: `get_issue` does not request `include=attachments`, and
`upload_file` was the only file method.

The `attachments` resource always lists every attachment of the issue. After
`download_attachments` each one has a status: `downloaded`, `not-selected`,
`skipped-too-large` or `failed` (with an `error`), and `filter` records the
selection. The size limit applies to the bytes Redmine serves as well as to the
size it records. A file served as an HTML page (a login or proxy error page) is
`failed`, not stored. If any download fails, the method stores the files that
did download and the resource, then fails the run and names each failed
attachment.

**Fixed:** Every request sent `X-Redmine-API-Key` and `X-Redmine-Username` to
whatever host a redirect pointed at, because `fetch` strips only
`Authorization` on a cross-origin redirect. Redirects are now followed by hand:
a same-origin redirect keeps the credentials, a cross-origin one (for example to
an S3 or CDN storage backend) is followed without them, and more than 5
redirects fail the request.

**Changed:** Requests no longer wait forever on a server that stops answering.
JSON requests time out after 120 seconds per attempt, downloads after 60 seconds
without data, and `upload_file`'s upload after 10 minutes per attempt.
`upload_file`'s upload now also retries 429/502/503/504 like every other call.

**Upgrade note:** No `globalArguments` changes; existing instances move to this
version with an identity upgrade. Downloads send `X-Redmine-Username` when
`username` is set, like every other method.

The ten iteration-1 fixes all hold up under probing, but the new redirect handling adds one HIGH regression: a request that is redirected to a different origin can now silently return anonymous results. There are also three MEDIUM and several LOW findings. Check, lint, fmt:check and test all pass (68 tests). Data-name collisions were left out, as you instructed.

**Fixes that hold up (probed directly):**
- **Redirects:** relative `Location` values resolve correctly. A malformed `Location` (`http://[::1`) is wrapped with the path and host. A 3xx without `Location` and a 304 both surface as `!ok`. Credential stripping persists after leaving the origin, including a later hop back. Bodies (JSON strings and the upload `Uint8Array`) are safe to reuse across hops and retries. One signal per attempt covers every hop.
- **Timeouts:** `AbortSignal.timeout` does cover `response.json()`. The idle timer is cleared in `finally` on every path. A stale timer from an earlier attempt cannot abort a retry: a 503 with Retry-After longer than the idle timeout, followed by a slow-but-live body, succeeded.
- **Buffering:** growth is correct. A declared `Content-Length: 0` with a non-empty body returns all of the body.
- **Status recording:** `filter` and status are written for both methods and validate against the schema.

### [HIGH] A cross-origin redirect silently turns API calls anonymous, including http→https on the same host
**File:** `redmine/extensions/models/redmine/_lib/api.ts` **Line(s):** 43, 74-77
**Issue:** `origin` includes the scheme and port, so an http→https upgrade on the same host drops `X-Redmine-API-Key`. A `redmine.corp`→`www.redmine.corp` hop does the same. The request is still followed, now without credentials. Before this branch, Deno's `fetch` kept that header on such a hop, so these setups worked.
**Breaking input:** `host: http://redmine.corp`, where nginx answers `301 https://redmine.corp/...`, and the instance allows anonymous read.
**Impact:**
- `list_issues`, `search` and `list_projects` silently return only the publicly visible subset.
- `get_issue` on a private issue returns 404, and authenticated endpoints return 401 with no hint that a redirect caused it.
- Silent wrong data is a data-integrity regression, and the release notes do not mention the change.
**Fix (either):**
- For the JSON helpers, throw on a cross-origin redirect with a clear message, e.g. `"<host> redirected to <origin>; set host to it"`. Only `redmineDownload` needs to follow credential-less hops (a presigned S3 or CDN URL).
- Treat a same-host http→https upgrade as credential-preserving.

Add a **Changed:** line to the release notes either way.

### [MEDIUM] The HTML-page guard rejects legitimate `.html` attachments and fails the whole run
**File:** `redmine.ts` **Line(s):** 2612-2622, 288
**Issue:** If Redmine records an empty `content_type` or `application/octet-stream`, the code falls back to `application/octet-stream`. Redmine's `detect_content_type` makes the same fallback but then resolves the type from the filename, so it serves `text/html` for `.html`/`.htm` files. The guard sees `text/html` served against a recorded `octet-stream` and marks the attachment `failed`, which then throws.
**Breaking input:** `report.html` uploaded through `/uploads.json` without `content_type` (`upload_file` does this when `contentType` is omitted), or a browser upload recorded as `application/octet-stream`.
**Impact:** A legitimate attachment can never be downloaded. The only way past it is to filter it out.
**Fix:** Also accept the file when the filename ends in `.html`/`.htm`. Better: detect a login or error page by `Content-Disposition` being absent (Redmine always sends `attachment` or `inline; filename=`) or by a `/login` path in the redirect chain, rather than by MIME mismatch alone.

### [MEDIUM] Throwing after writing contradicts the swamp model guidance, and one partial-failure path is still unrecorded
**File:** `redmine.ts` **Line(s):** 2636-2681
**Issue:** `api.md` ("Error Handling", lines 504-507) says: "Throw **before** writing data — failed executions should not persist incorrect or misleading data." This method writes files and the resource, then throws, so the run returns no `dataHandles`. Separately, if `writer.writeAll` throws partway through the loop, earlier files are persisted but the resource is never written, so that partial failure goes unrecorded despite the new design.
**Breaking input:** A disk-full or permission error on the second attachment's `writeAll`.
**Impact:** The resource is honest, but the design deviates from documented platform semantics, and that is your call to make, not an agent's. The `writeAll` path also silently breaks the "resource is always written" claim in the README and release notes.
**Fix:** Get your explicit approval on throw-after-write, or switch to returning success with `failed` entries. Either way, catch `writeAll` errors per attachment and record them as `failed`.

### [MEDIUM] `dataName` names files that were never downloaded, or older versions of them
**File:** `redmine.ts` **Line(s):** 294, 2594, 2598, 2626-2633, schema 889-892
**Issue:** Every entry carries `dataName` (described as "Data name of the stored file") even when its status is `listed`, `not-selected`, `skipped-too-large` or `failed`.
**Breaking input:** Run 1 downloads attachment 3. In run 2 it returns a 404 (status `failed`). `data.latest(def, "attachment-5-3")` still returns run 1's file, while the resource says it failed. For entries never downloaded, the name points at nothing.
**Impact:** A consumer that follows `dataName` without checking `status` reads stale or missing data.
**Fix:** Make `dataName` nullable (an additive change) and set it only for `downloaded`. Or document that it is valid only when `status === "downloaded"`.

### [LOW] A timeout while reading a JSON body is not wrapped
**File:** `api.ts` **Line(s):** 163, 227; `redmine.ts` 2478
**Issue:** `response.json()` on the success path sits outside the `try`. The probe produced a bare `TimeoutError: The operation was aborted due to timeout`, with no method, path or host.
**Breaking input:** A server that sends headers and then stalls the body for more than 120 s.
**Fix:** Wrap the success-path `.json()` the same way the fetch call is wrapped.

### [LOW] Retrying `POST /uploads.json` can leave orphan uploads
**File:** `redmine.ts` **Line(s):** 2449-2453
**Issue:** On a 502 or 504 after Redmine has already stored the upload, the retry stores a second one. The orphan rows and files stay until an admin runs `redmine:attachments:prune`, which is not automatic. Worst-case wall time is about 5 × 10 min plus backoff.
**Impact:** Disk waste only; the token from the successful retry is the one attached.
**Note:** The same retry rule already applied to `POST /issues.json` before this branch (2026.09.19.1). There, a retried 502 or 504 can create a duplicate issue, which is worse.

### [LOW] A huge declared `Content-Length` is allocated before any byte arrives
**File:** `api.ts` **Line(s):** 331-333
**Issue:** The buffer is allocated at the declared size up front.
**Breaking input:** A user sets `maxBytes` to 500 MiB, and a server declares `Content-Length: 524288000`, then sends nothing or closes.
**Impact:** 500 MiB is allocated per attachment before the failure. It is mostly virtual memory and runs one attachment at a time.
**Fix:** Cap the initial allocation (e.g. `min(declared, 8 MiB)`) and grow from there.

### [LOW] `filter` does not record `maxBytes`
**File:** `redmine.ts` **Line(s):** 2652-2655
**Issue:** `skipped-too-large` depends on `maxBytes`, but the resource does not record the value used.
**Fix:** Add a nullable `maxBytes` to `filter`. This is an additive change.

### [LOW] Test gaps: reverting some fixes would hang the tests or leave them passing
**File:** `api_test.ts`, `redmine_test.ts`
- **Idle-timeout test:** it asserts only `"failed while reading the body"`, not `"no data for 50ms"`. With the timer removed the test would hang rather than fail.
- **No test covers the 120 s JSON timeout default.** Removing `AbortSignal.timeout` from `redmineFetch` would fail nothing.
- **Missing redirect cases:** a scheme change, a hop back to the origin after leaving it, a 301 POST being rewritten to GET, and a malformed `Location`.
- **Missing download cases:** a retry with a fresh controller, and a `writeAll` failure.

**Docs:** Every claim in the README and the top release-notes entry matches the code, with three exceptions:
- "more than 5 redirects fail" is accurate, but the release notes say nothing about credentials being dropped on scheme or host changes (the HIGH finding).
- The "an HTML page served in place of the file" claim over-applies (the first MEDIUM finding).
- "writes the attachments resource" is not true on a `writeAll` failure (the second MEDIUM finding).

No TODOs or deferred work markers were found in the diff.

**Instance name uniqueness:** Instance names map directly to storage paths on
disk. If two different specs use the same instance name (e.g.,
`writeResource("summary", "bixu", ...)` and
`writeResource("repo", "bixu", ...)`), the second write overwrites the first.
When a behavior has multiple resource specs, prefix instance names with the spec
name or use another strategy to ensure uniqueness across all specs within a
method execution.

```typescript
// Wrong — "bixu" collides across specs on disk
await context.writeResource("summary", "bixu", summaryData);
await context.writeResource("repo", "bixu", repoData); // overwrites!

// Correct — prefix ensures unique storage paths
await context.writeResource("summary", `summary-${user}`, summaryData);
await context.writeResource("repo", `repo-${repo}`, repoData);
```

**ResourceWriteOverrides** (optional):

| Field               | Description                                    |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `lifetime`          | Override lifetime (default from spec)          |
| `garbageCollection` | Override version retention (default from spec) |
| `tags`              | Additional tags                                |

**Example:**

```typescript
// Single-instance resource (use descriptive instance name)
const handle = await context.writeResource("state", "current", {
  status: "active",
  updatedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
This error occurs when two `writeResource` or `createFileWriter` calls within
the same method execution use the same instance name, even across different
specs. Instance names map to storage paths on disk — the path has no spec
component, so `writeResource("summary", "bixu", ...)` and
`writeResource("repo", "bixu", ...)` both write to the same `bixu/` directory,
and the second overwrites the first.

**Fix:** Use unique instance names across all specs within a method. Prefix with
the spec name or another distinguishing value:

```typescript
// Wrong — same instance name across specs
await context.writeResource("summary", user.name, summaryData);
await context.writeResource("repo", repo.name, repoData);
// Fails when user.name === repo.name (e.g., both are "bixu")

// Correct — prefix ensures uniqueness
await context.writeResource("summary", `summary-${user.name}`, summaryData);
await context.writeResource("repo", `repo-${repo.name}`, repoData);
```

# generic client that emits one flat envelope per call (per project
            # for MRs/commits, per MR for notes); the collector groups by the
            # envelope's project/noteableIid internally. Add one array entry per
            # gitlab instance you run. Example wires a single project "100".
            mergeRequestLists:
              - ${{ data.latest("gitlab", "100-opened").attributes }}
            mrNotesLists: []
            commitLists:
              - ${{ data.latest("gitlab", "100-commits").attributes }}
            crewReference: ${{ data.latest("crew-reference", "reference-current").attributes }}
        dependsOn: []

      - name: collect-redmine
        description: Translate Redmine issue journals into events
        allowFailure: true
        task:
          type: model_method
          modelIdOrName: collect-redmine
          methodName: sync
          inputs:
            # Array of @webframp/redmine get_issue detail records (self-contained:
            # project, author, journals). One array entry per get_issue instance.
            issues:
              - ${{ data.latest("redmine", "issue-7").attributes }}
            crewReference: ${{ data.latest("crew-reference", "reference-current").attributes }}
        dependsOn: []

      - name: collect-teams
        description: Translate Teams channel messages into events
        allowFailure: true
        task:
          type: model_method
          modelIdOrName: collect-teams
          methodName: sync
          inputs:
            # Array of @webframp/microsoft/teams channelMessages envelopes (each
            # { channelId, messages[] }). One array entry per channel instance.
            channels:
              - ${{ data.latest("teams", "chan-1").attributes }}
            crewReference: ${{ data.latest("crew-reference", "reference-current").attributes }}
        dependsOn: []

## 2026.10.20.1

**Added:** `list_attachments` lists the attachments of an issue (ID, file name,
size, content type, author, date) into a new `attachments` resource, named
`attachments-<issueId>`. `download_attachments` downloads them in one run into a
new `attachment` file spec, named `attachment-<issueId>-<attachmentId>`. It
filters by attachment IDs or a content-type prefix (case-insensitive) and skips
files over `maxBytes` (default 20 MiB). Until now the type had no way to read an
attachment.

The `attachments` resource always lists every attachment of the issue, with a
status (`downloaded`, `not-selected`, `skipped-too-large` or `failed` with an
`error`) and, for downloaded ones, the `dataName` of the stored file. `filter`
records the selection and `maxBytes`. The size limit applies to the bytes
Redmine serves as well as to the size it records. A non-HTML attachment served
as an HTML page (a login or proxy error page) is `failed`, not stored. If any
download fails, the method stores the files that did download and the resource,
then fails the run naming each failed attachment.

**Fixed:** Every request sent `X-Redmine-API-Key` and `X-Redmine-Username` to
whatever host a redirect pointed at, because `fetch` strips only
`Authorization` on a cross-origin redirect.

**Fixed:** Methods overwrote each other's stored data. Swamp stores data by
name, not by spec, so `list_statuses`, `list_trackers`, `list_projects` and
`list_custom_fields` all wrote `all`, and `get_issue` and `list_relations` both
wrote the bare issue ID. Every data name now carries a spec prefix (see
**Upgrade note**).

**Fixed:** The source files' SPDX header said AGPL-3.0-or-later; it now says
Apache-2.0, matching `LICENSE.md` and the manifest.

**Changed:** A redirect to another origin now fails an API call with a message
naming the URL to set as `host`. A same-origin redirect, or an http→https
upgrade of the same host, still works. `download_attachments` follows other
redirects without the credentials (S3 or CDN storage backends).

**Changed:** A POST (`create_issue`, `create_version`, `upload_file`, ...)
retries only a 429. A 502 or 504 can arrive after Redmine already created the
record, and retrying it created a duplicate. GET, PUT and DELETE still retry
429/502/503/504. `upload_file`'s upload now uses the same retry and redirect
handling as every other call.

**Changed:** Requests no longer wait forever on a server that stops answering.
JSON requests time out after 120 seconds per attempt, downloads after 60
seconds without data, and `upload_file`'s upload after 10 minutes per attempt.

**Upgrade note:** Data names change. Update any `data.latest(...)` or
`model.<name>.resource.<spec>.<name>` reference:

- `all` → `statuses-all`, `trackers-all`, `projects-all`, `custom-fields-all`
- `<project>` → `users-<project>`, `versions-<project>`,
  `issue-categories-<project>`
- `<filters>` → `issues-<filters>`; `<issueId>` → `issue-<issueId>`,
  `relations-<issueId>`; `<versionId>` → `version-<versionId>`
- time entries → `time-entries-<...>`; search → `search-<query>`

Data stored under the old names is not migrated; rerun the method to write it
under the new name. No `globalArguments` changes.

EOF

Review iteration 3 is running on commit `290eb0fd`.

Since your last answers, I've made these changes:
- **License header:** both SPDX headers now say Apache-2.0.
- **Data names:** every resource name now carries its spec prefix. This fixed four list methods that all wrote `"all"`, and `get_issue`/`list_relations`, which overwrote each other. It also makes the devops-measurement workflow's existing `data.latest("redmine", "issue-7")` reference resolve. The release notes list each old and new name in an upgrade note.
- **Redirects:** API calls now fail on a cross-origin redirect instead of silently returning anonymous results. An http→https upgrade on the same host still works. Downloads follow other redirects with the credentials stripped.
- **POST retries:** POSTs retry only on 429. Retrying a 502 or 504 could create a duplicate issue; that bug dates from the 2026.09.19.1 retry change.
- **Smaller fixes:** `.html` attachments recorded without a type now download, storage failures are recorded per attachment, and `dataName` is set only for downloaded files.
- **Release notes:** the file now holds only the current version, per the repo's overwrite rule.

<result>## Adversarial review: @webframp/redmine 2026.10.20.1 (iteration 3)

Gates: `deno task check`, `lint`, `fmt:check` and `test` (78 passed) all pass. `swamp extension quality` returns `passed` at 100%.

Consumer breakage from the rename: none.
- The devops-measurement workflow's `data.latest("redmine", "issue-7")` now matches the new `get_issue` name. Before this PR it read `7`, so the reference was broken and this PR fixes it.
- redmine-kanban reports and the operator-briefing normalizer find data by `handle.name`, so a renamed name is picked up automatically.
- No skill, workflow or doc refers to an old name.

Data names never collide across specs. Every spec prefix is distinct: `issue-<int>` vs `issues-`, `version-<int>` vs `versions-`, `attachment-` vs `attachments-`, and `issue-categories-` vs `issue-<digits>` all separate. swamp's docs list no reserved names. The README table matches all 19 `writeResource`/`createFileWriter` calls, and the method count of 28 matches.

Mutation testing: I made one change at a time in a scratch copy and reran the suite.
- Three changes left every test passing: `redmineDownload` using `reject`, removing the http→https upgrade branch, and reverting `upload_file` to plain `fetch`.
- Two changes failed tests, as they should: removing the POST policy and keeping `Content-Type` after a method rewrite.

### HIGH: PUTs that add data are still retried on 502/504, which duplicates journal notes
**File:** `redmine/extensions/models/redmine/_lib/api.ts` (lines 13-20); `redmine/extensions/models/redmine/redmine.ts` (`update_issue`'s PUT around line 1540; `upload_file`'s attach PUT around line 2527)
**Issue:** The PR limits POST retries to 429 because "a 502 or 504 can arrive after Redmine already created the record". That reasoning applies just as much to `PUT /issues/:id.json` with `notes`: every successful PUT creates a new journal entry. `isRetryableStatus` still retries PUT on 502/503/504, and both RELEASE_NOTES.md and the README now present this as correct ("GET, PUT and DELETE still retry 429/502/503/504").
**Breaking input:** Run `update_issue` with `notes: "deployed"`. Redmine saves the journal, then a proxy returns 504. The retry posts the note again, up to 4 duplicate comments in total.
**Impact:** Duplicate comments on real tickets. This is the same root cause the PR fixes for POST, so it falls under the user's in-scope rule.
**Fix:** Retry only on 429 for any method other than GET or HEAD. Alternatively, pass a per-call `idempotent` flag, so `update_journal` and `update_version` can keep 5xx retries while `update_issue` with notes and the upload attach step cannot. Correct the release notes and README to match, and add a test.

### MEDIUM: Retrying a DELETE after a 502/504 reports failure for a delete that succeeded
**File:** `_lib/api.ts` line 19
**Issue:** If Redmine deletes the issue, relation, version or watcher and a proxy then returns 502, the retry gets a 404 and `redmineApi` throws.
**Breaking input:** `delete_issue` when the gateway times out after the delete has committed.
**Impact:** The workflow step fails although the record is gone. A re-run fails again with 404.
**Fix:** Either stop retrying DELETE on 5xx, or treat a 404 on a DELETE retry as success.

### MEDIUM: Distinct inputs to the same method still overwrite each other's data
**File:** `redmine.ts` line 2068 (`search`) and lines 1884-1890 (`list_time_entries`)
**Issue:** CLAUDE.md requires instance names to be collision-resistant (hash variable inputs). The PR fixes overwrites across methods and claims every name is now safe, but overwrites within a method remain:
- `search` replaces every non-alphanumeric character and truncates to 50 characters, so `foo bar`, `foo-bar` and `foo_bar` all write `search-foo_bar`. Any two queries sharing their first 50 characters also collide.
- `list_time_entries` ignores `userId`, `from` and `to`, so different users and date ranges all write `time-entries-all` or `time-entries-<project>`.
- `issueId: 5` and `project: "5"` (a numeric project ID) both write `time-entries-5`.
**Impact:** A later run silently replaces data from different inputs. This is the overwrite defect the PR fixes, inside one method.
**Fix:** Append a short SHA-1 of the normalized arguments, for example `search-<sanitized>-<hash8>`, and include every filter in the time-entries name.

### MEDIUM: `upload_file`'s move to `redmineFetch` is untested
**File:** `redmine/extensions/models/redmine/redmine_test.ts`
**Issue:** Reverting the upload to plain `fetch(...)` (mutation M3) passes all 78 tests. Nothing checks that the upload rejects a cross-origin redirect instead of sending `X-Redmine-API-Key`, that it skips 502 retries, or that it gets a timeout signal.
**Impact:** The credential-leak and duplicate-upload fixes for this call path can regress unnoticed.
**Fix:** Add `upload_file` tests for a cross-origin 307 (rejected, the other server gets no request), a 502 (exactly one request), and a 429 (retried).

### MEDIUM: Downloads following S3/CDN redirects are untested at the download level
**File:** `_lib/api_test.ts`, `redmine_test.ts`
**Issue:** Changing `redmineDownload` to `crossOrigin: "reject"` (mutation M1) passes every test. Strip mode is only tested by calling `redmineFetch` directly.
**Impact:** A regression would quietly break `download_attachments` on any Redmine whose storage redirects to S3 or a CDN.
**Fix:** Add a `redmineDownload` or `download_attachments` test where the origin returns 302 to a second server. Assert that the bytes come back and the second server sees no credential headers.

### LOW: The http→https upgrade branch inside the redirect loop is untested
**File:** `_lib/api.ts` lines 98-100
**Issue:** Replacing `if (isHttpsUpgrade(...))` with `if (false)` (mutation M2) passes. Only the predicate has a unit test. A fetch-mock test (stub `globalThis.fetch` to answer an `http://` URL with 301 to `https://` on the same host) would cover the loop without TLS.

### LOW: Two tests are named for behavior they don't check
**File:** `_lib/api_test.ts`
**Issue:**
- "gives each attempt a signal" makes a single attempt (`seen.length === 1`). Building one signal outside the retry loop would still pass.
- "also after a hop back" begins on `other`, so it never returns to the origin it left. Removing `leftOrigin` entirely (mutation M7) passes, and that mutation is equivalent, because `headers.delete` already persists across hops. So `leftOrigin` is effectively dead code.
**Fix:** Make the first test do a 429 then a 200 and assert two distinct signals. Fix the second scenario, or drop `leftOrigin`.

### LOW: The release notes and README undercount the old name collisions and leave out `listed`
**File:** `redmine/RELEASE_NOTES.md`, `redmine/README.md` "Data names" section
**Issue:**
- Besides the four lookup methods, `list_issues` and `list_time_entries` with no filters also wrote `all`.
- `list_time_entries` with `issueId` also wrote the bare issue ID, and `get_version`/`create_version` wrote bare version IDs that could collide with issue IDs.
- The upgrade note's `all →` bullet leaves out `issues-all` and `time-entries-all`.
- The status lists in both files omit `listed`, which is what `list_attachments` writes.
- Length is 3234 characters, under the 5000 limit, and the format is fine.
**Fix:** Complete both lists.

### LOW: The root README's method count is stale
**File:** `README.md` lines 111 and 383
**Issue:** It says "26 methods"; the extension now has 28.

### LOW: `_lib/api.ts` has no SPDX header
**File:** `redmine/extensions/models/redmine/_lib/api.ts`
**Issue:** This file is shipped, but it carries no license header, while `redmine.ts` and both test files now say Apache-2.0. The release-note line "The source files' SPDX header said AGPL" only applied to `redmine.ts`.

Nothing else turned up:

### Redirects, retries and timeouts

Redirects are followed by hand. A same-origin redirect, or an http→https upgrade
of the same host, keeps `X-Redmine-API-Key` and `X-Redmine-Username`. Any other
redirect fails an API call with a message naming the URL to set as `host`;
`download_attachments` follows it without the credentials, for storage backends
that redirect to S3 or a CDN. A POST (`create_issue`, `create_version`,
`upload_file`, ...) retries only a 429, since a 502 or 504 can arrive after
Redmine already created the record. JSON requests time out after 120 seconds per
attempt, downloads after 60 seconds without data, and `upload_file`'s upload
after 10 minutes per attempt.

### Data names


Swamp stores data by name with no spec component, so every name carries a spec
prefix. Before 2026.10.20.1, `list_statuses`, `list_trackers`, `list_projects`
and `list_custom_fields` all wrote `all`, and `get_issue` and `list_relations`
both wrote the bare issue ID, overwriting one another.

| Method                                      | Spec               | Data name                                |

3800 RELEASE_NOTES.md
 README.md | 285 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++-------------------------------
 1 file changed, 143 insertions(+), 142 deletions(-)

**Fixed:** Every request sent `X-Redmine-API-Key` and `X-Redmine-Username` to
whatever host a redirect pointed at, because `fetch` strips only `Authorization`
on a cross-origin redirect.

**Fixed:** Methods overwrote each other's stored data. Swamp stores data by
name, not by spec. `list_statuses`, `list_trackers`, `list_projects`,
`list_custom_fields`, and unfiltered `list_issues` and `list_time_entries` all
wrote `all`. `get_issue`, `list_relations`, `list_time_entries` by issue and
`get_version` wrote bare numeric IDs. `list_users`, `list_versions`,
`list_time_entries` and `list_issue_categories` wrote the bare project. Within
one method, `list_time_entries` ignored the user and date filters, and `search`
mapped `foo bar` and `foo-bar` to the same name. Every data name now carries a
spec prefix and every filter (see **Upgrade note**).

**Fixed:** `redmine.ts` and its test said
`SPDX-License-Identifier:
AGPL-3.0-or-later`; every source file now says
Apache-2.0, matching `LICENSE.md` and the manifest.

**Changed:** A redirect to another origin now fails an API call with a message
naming the URL to set as `host`. A same-origin redirect, or an http→https
upgrade of the same host, still works. `download_attachments` follows other
redirects without the credentials (S3 or CDN storage backends).

**Changed:** Only reads (GET) retry a 502, 503 or 504. A gateway can time out
after Redmine committed a write, so retrying created a duplicate issue or
upload, added a second journal note, or reported a 404 for a delete that
succeeded. Every method still retries a 429. `upload_file`'s upload now uses the
same retry and redirect handling as every other call.

**Changed:** Requests no longer wait forever on a server that stops answering.
JSON requests time out after 120 seconds per attempt, downloads after 60 seconds
without data, and `upload_file`'s upload after 10 minutes per attempt.

**Upgrade note:** Data names change. Update any `data.latest(...)` or
`model.<name>.resource.<spec>.<name>` reference:

- `all` → `statuses-all`, `trackers-all`, `projects-all`, `custom-fields-all`,
  `issues-all`, `time-entries-all`
- `<project>` → `users-<project>`, `versions-<project>`,
  `issue-categories-<project>`
- `<filters>` → `issues-<filters>`; `<issueId>` → `issue-<issueId>`,
  `relations-<issueId>`; `<versionId>` → `version-<versionId>`
- time entries → `time-entries-<filters>` (e.g. `time-entries-i:42`,
  `time-entries-p:web-u:3`); search → `search-<query>-<hash>`

Data stored under the old names is not migrated; rerun the method to write it
under the new name. No `globalArguments` changes.

message.

function isRetryableStatus(status: number, method: string): boolean {

function isRetryableStatus(response: Response, method: string): boolean {

}'''),
